rationale: Engineering managers and product leads at 5–200 person AI-assisted dev shops are a nameable B2B buyer with real budget (they pay for GitHub Copilot, Linear, Jira), and the pain — AI-generated code drifting from spec — is frequent and genuinely costly. Willingness to pay sits at the minimum floor (5): there are adjacent paid tools (PR review bots, spec linters) but no dominant paid incumbent specifically for AI-drift detection, so the price signal is indirect. The total of 5.5 is just at the validate threshold; no build gates are triggered since stage is validate. The deciding factor is weak responsiveness signal — this HN thread is a single philosophical comment, not a chorus of buyers saying 'I need this now.' Run a 20-outreach test to eng managers on LinkedIn before investing further.
solution_plan: The micro-service is a spec-drift checker: paste your user story / PRD snippet and your AI-generated code diff, get a structured report on what's aligned, what's missing, and what contradicts the spec. The factory builds a Claude prompt that takes (spec text + code diff) as input, a simple web form (no login required initially), and a Stripe pay-per-report link ($5-9 per check) or a $29/month subscription for teams — no coding by Youval. Sell by reaching engineering managers in AI-dev communities (Slack groups for Cursor/Copilot users, r/ExperiencedDevs, dev-focused LinkedIn) with a free first report offer; outreach batch goes out only after Youval approves it. Delivery is fully automated: user submits form → Claude runs the check → PDF/markdown report delivered by email within minutes; billing via Stripe. The only recurring human touch is approving outreach batches and monitoring for abuse. The weak point is defensibility — any competitor can clone the prompt — so speed-to-distribution and early data on what specs commonly drift matters.
notes: No build gates fail at validate stage. If total rises above 6.5 in future scoring, re-check operational_autonomy (currently 6, at floor) before promoting to build.
